entries.bfd11bcff443675f86667be76187a92e51ff633b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv100"/><title type="x-ms">Micah</title> <div sID="gen20386" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">We</hi> shall have some account of this prophet in the first verse of the book of his prophecy; and therefore shall here only observe that, being contemporary with the prophet Isaiah (only that he began to prophesy a little after him), there is a near resemblance between that prophet's prophecy and this; and there is a prediction of the advancement and establishment of the gospel-church, which both of them have, almost in the same words, that out of the mouth of two such witnesses so great a word might be established. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 2, 3, with Mic. iv. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.2">2</reference>. Isaiah's prophecy is said to be concerning <hi type="italic">Judah and Jerusalem,</hi> but Micah's concerning <hi type="italic">Samaria and Jerusalem;</hi> for, though this prophecy be dated only by the reigns of the kings of Judah, yet it refers to the kingdom of Israel, the approaching ruin of which, in the captivity of the ten tribes, he plainly foretels and sadly laments. What we find here in writing was but an abstract of the sermons he preached during the reigns of three kings. The scope of the whole is, I. To convince sinners of their sins, by setting them in order before them, charging both Israel and Judah with idolatry, covetousness, oppression, contempt of the word of God, and their rulers especially, both in church and state, with the abuse of their power; and also by showing them the judgments of God ready to break in upon them for their sins. II. To comfort God's people with promises of mercy and deliverance, especially with an assurance of the coming of the Messiah and of the grace of the gospel through him. It is remarkable concerning this prophecy, and confirms its authority, that we find two quotations out of it made publicly upon very solemn occasions, and both referring to very great events. 1. One is a prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">ch. iii. 12</reference>), which we find quoted in the Old Testament, by <hi type="italic">the elders of the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.17-Jer.26.18">Jer. xxvi. 17, 18</reference>), in justification of Jeremiah, when he foretold the judgments of God coming upon Jerusalem, and to stay the proceedings of the court against him. "Micah (say they) foretold that <hi type="italic">Zion should be ploughed as a field,</hi> and Hezekiah did not put him to death; why then should we punish Jeremiah for saying the same?" 2. Another is a prediction of the birth of Christ (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">ch. v. 2</reference>) which we find quoted in the New Testament, by the <hi type="italic">chief priests and scribes of the people,</hi> in answer to Herod's enquiry, <hi type="italic">where Christ should be born</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.5-Matt.2.6">Matt. ii. 5, 6</reference>); for still we find that to him bear all the prophets witness. <div eID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20388" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The title of the book (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">ver. 1</reference>) and a preface demanding attention, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. Warning given of desolating judgments hastening upon the kingdoms of Israel and Judah (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.3-Mic.1.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), and all for sin, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. The particulars of the destruction specified, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.6-Mic.1.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. The greatness of the destruction illustrated, 1. By the prophet's sorrow for it, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.8-Mic.1.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. 2. By the general sorrow that should be for it, in the several places that must expect to share in it, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.10-Mic.1.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. These prophecies of Micah might well be called his lamentations. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv100"/> <div eID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20388" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 743.)</title> <div sID="gen20390" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear, all ye people; hearken, O earth, and all that therein is: and let the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. <hi type="super">3</hi> For, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> cometh forth out of his place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as the waters <hi type="italic">that are</hi> poured down a steep place. <hi type="super">5</hi> For the transgression of Jacob <hi type="italic">is</hi> all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What <hi type="italic">is</hi> the transgression of Jacob? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> not Samaria? and what <hi type="italic">are</hi> the high places of Judah? <hi type="italic">are they</hi> not Jerusalem? <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore I will make Samaria as a heap of the field, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. <hi type="super">7</hi> And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces, and all the hires thereof shall be burned with the fire, and all the idols thereof will I lay desolate: for she gathered <hi type="italic">it</hi> of the hire of a harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot. <div eID="gen20390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20391" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general account of this prophet and his prophecy, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">v. 1</reference>. This is prefixed for the satisfaction of all that read and hear the prophecy of this book, who will give the more credit to it when they know the author and his authority. 1. The prophecy is the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord;</hi> it is a divine revelation. Note, What is written in the Bible, and what is preached by the ministers of Christ according to what is written there, must be heard and received, not as the word of dying men, which we may be judges of, but as the word of the living God, which we must be judged by, for so it is. This word of the Lord came to the prophet, came plainly, came powerfully, came in a preventing way, and he saw it, saw the vision in which it was conveyed to him, saw the things themselves which he foretold, with as much clearness and certainty as if they had been already accomplished. 2. The prophet is Micah the Morasthite; his name <hi type="italic">Micah</hi> is a contraction of Micaiah, the name of a prophet some ages before (in Ahab's time, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">1 Kings xxii. 8</reference>); his surname, the <hi type="italic">Morasthite,</hi> signifies that he was born, or lived, at Moresheth, which is mentioned here (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.14">v. 14</reference>), or Mareshah, which is mentioned <reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">and Josh. xv. 44</reference>. The place of his abode is mentioned, that any one might enquire in that place, at that time, and might find there was, or had been, such a one there, who was generally reputed to be a prophet. 3. The date of his prophecy is in the reigns of three kings of Judah—Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Ahaz was one of the worst of Judah's kings, and Hezekiah one of the best; such variety of times pass over God's ministers, times that frown and times that smile, to each of which they must study to accommodate themselves, and to arm themselves against the temptations of both. The promises and threatenings of this book are interwoven, by which it appears that even in the wicked reign he preached comfort, and said <hi type="italic">to the righteous</hi> then that it should be <hi type="italic">well with them;</hi> and that in the pious reign he preached conviction, and said to the wicked then that it should be <hi type="italic">ill with them;</hi> for, however the times change, the word of the Lord is still the same. 4. The parties concerned in this prophecy; it is <hi type="italic">concerning Samaria and Jerusalem,</hi> the head cities of the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, under the influence of which the kingdoms themselves were. Though the ten tribes have deserted the houses both of David and Aaron, yet God is pleased to send prophets to them. <div eID="gen20391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20392" type="x-p"/> II. A very solemn introduction to the following prophecy (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.2">v. 2</reference>), in which, 1. The people are summoned to draw near and give their attendance, as upon a court of judicature: <hi type="italic">Hear, all you people,</hi> Note, Where God has a mouth to speak we must have an ear to hear; we all must, for we are all concerned in what is delivered. "<hi type="italic">Hear, you people" (all of them,</hi> so the margin reads it), "all you that are now within hearing, and all others that hear it at second hand." It is an unusual construction; but those words with which Micah begins his prophecy are the very same in the original with those wherewith Micaiah ended his, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.28">1 Kings xxii. 28</reference>. 2. The earth is called upon, with <hi type="italic">all that therein is,</hi> to hear what the prophet has to say: <hi type="italic">Hearken, O earth!</hi> The earth shall be made to shake under the stroke and weight of the judgments coming; sooner will the earth hear than this stupid senseless people; but God will be heard when he pleads. If the church, and those in it, will not hear, the earth, and those in it, shall, and shame them. 3. God himself is appealed to, and his omniscience, power, and justice, are vouched in testimony against this people: "<hi type="italic">Let the Lord God be witness against you,</hi> a witness that you had fair warning given you, that your prophets did their duty faithfully as watchmen, but you would not take the warning; let the accomplishment of the prophecy be a witness against your contempt and disbelief of it, and prove, to your conviction and confusion, that it was the word of God, and no word of his shall fall to the ground." Note, God himself will be a witness, by the judgments of his hand, against those that would not receive his testimony in the judgments of his mouth. He will be a witness <hi type="italic">from his holy temple</hi> in heaven, when he comes down to execute judgment (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">v. 3</reference>) against those that turned a deaf ear to his oracles, wherein he witnessed to them, out of his holy temple at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen20392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20393" type="x-p"/> III. A terrible prediction of destroying judgments which should come upon Judah and Israel, which had its accomplishment soon after in Israel, and at length in Judah; for it is foretold, 1. That God himself will appear against them, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">v. 3</reference>. They boasted of themselves and their relation to God, as if that would secure them; but, though God never deceives the faith of the upright, he will disappoint the presumption of the hypocrites, for, <hi type="italic">behold, the Lord comes forth out of his place,</hi> quits his mercy-seat, where they thought they had him fast, and prepares his throne for judgment; his glory departs, for they drive it from them. God's way towards this people had long been a way of mercy, but now he changes his way, he <hi type="italic">comes out of his place,</hi> and will come down. He had seemed to retire, as one regardless of what was done, but now he will show himself, he will <hi type="italic">rend the heavens,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">come down,</hi> not as sometimes, in surprising mercies, but in surprising judgments, to do things not for them, but against them, which they <hi type="italic">looked not for,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa. lxiv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">xxvi. 21</reference>. 2. That when the Creator appears against them it shall be in vain for any creature to appear for them. He will <hi type="italic">tread</hi> with contempt and disdain <hi type="italic">upon the high places of the</hi> earth, upon all the powers that are advanced in competition with him or in opposition to him; and he will so tread upon them as to tread them down and level them. High places, set up for the worship of idols or for military fortifications, shall all be trodden down and trampled into the dust. Do men trust to the height and strength of the mountains and rocks, as if they were sufficient to bear up their hopes and bear off their fears? They shall be <hi type="italic">molten under him,</hi> melted down <hi type="italic">as wax before the fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2">Ps. lxviii. 2</reference>. Do they trust to the fruitfulness of the valleys, and their products? They <hi type="italic">shall be cleft,</hi> or rent, with those <hi type="italic">fiery streams</hi> that shall come pouring down from the mountains when they are melted. They shall be ploughed and washed away as the ground is by <hi type="italic">the waters that are poured down a steep place.</hi> God is said to <hi type="italic">cleave the earth with rivers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Hab. iii. 9</reference>. Neither men of <hi type="italic">high degree,</hi> as the mountains, nor <hi type="italic">men of low degree,</hi> as the valleys, shall be able to secure either themselves or the land from judgments of God, when they are sent with commission to lay all waste, and, like <hi type="italic">a sweeping rain,</hi> to <hi type="italic">leave no food,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.3">Prov. xxviii. 3</reference>. This is applied particularly to the head city of Israel, which they hoped would be a protection to the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.6">v. 6</reference>): I <hi type="italic">will make Samaria,</hi> that is now a rich and populous city, as <hi type="italic">a heap of the field,</hi> as a heap of dung laid there to be spread, or as a heap of stones gathered together to be carried away, and <hi type="italic">as plantings of a vineyard,</hi> as hillocks of earth raised to plant vines in. God will make of that <hi type="italic">city a heap,</hi> of that <hi type="italic">defenced city a ruin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa. xxv. 2</reference>. Their <hi type="italic">altars</hi> had been as <hi type="italic">heaps in the furrows of the fields</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Hos. xii. 11</reference>) and now their houses shall be so, as ruinous heaps. The <hi type="italic">stones of the city</hi> are <hi type="italic">poured down into the valley</hi> by the fury of the conqueror, who will thus be revenged on those walls that so long held out against him. They shall be quite pulled down, so that the very <hi type="italic">foundations</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">discovered,</hi> that had been covered by the superstructure; and not one stone shall be left upon another. <div eID="gen20393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20394" type="x-p"/> IV. A charge of sin upon them, as the procuring cause of these desolating judgments (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">For the transgression of Jacob is all this.</hi> If it be asked, "Why is God so angry, and why are Jacob and Israel thus brought to ruin by his anger?" the answer is ready: Sin has done all the mischief; sin has laid all waste; all the calamities of Jacob and Israel are owing to their transgressions; if they had not gone away from God, he would never have appeared thus against them. Note, External privileges and professions will not secure a sinful people from the judgments of God. If sin be found in the <hi type="italic">house of Israel,</hi> if Jacob be guilty of transgression and rebellion, God will not spare them; no, he will punish them first, for their sins are of all others most provoking to him, for they are most reproaching. But it is asked, <hi type="italic">What is the transgression of Jacob?</hi> Note, When we feel the smart of sin it concerns us to enquire what the sin is which we smart for, that we may particularly war against that which wars against us. And what is it? 1. It is idolatry; it is the <hi type="italic">high places;</hi> that is the transgression, the great transgression which reigns in Israel; that is spiritual whoredom, the violation of the marriage-covenant, which merits a divorce. Even the <hi type="italic">high places of Judah,</hi> though not so bad as the transgression of Jacob, were yet offensive enough to God, and a remaining blemish upon some of the good reigns. <hi type="italic">Howbeit the high places were not taken away.</hi> 2. It is the idolatry of Samaria and Jerusalem, the royal cities of those two kingdoms. These were the most populous places, and where there were most people there was most wickedness, and they made one another worse. These were the most pompous places; there men lived most in wealth and pleasure, and they forgot God. These were the places that had the greatest influence upon the country, by authority and example; so that from them idolatry and <hi type="italic">profaneness went forth throughout all the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.15">Jer. xxiii. 15</reference>. Note, Spiritual distempers are most contagious in persons and places that are most conspicuous. If the head city of a kingdom, or the chief family in a parish, be vicious and profane, <hi type="italic">many will follow their pernicious ways,</hi> and write after a bad copy when great ones set it for them. The vices of leaders and rulers are leading ruling vices, and therefore shall be surely and sorely punished. Those have a great deal to answer for indeed that not only sin, but <hi type="italic">make Israel to sin.</hi> Those must expect to be made examples that have been examples of wickedness. If the transgression of Jacob is Samaria, therefore shall <hi type="italic">Samaria become a heap.</hi> Let the ringleaders in sin hear this and fear. <div eID="gen20394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20395" type="x-p"/> V. The punishment made to answer the sin, in the particular destruction of the idols, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.7">v. 7</reference>. 1. The gods they worshipped shall be destroyed: <hi type="italic">The graven images shall be beaten to pieces</hi> by the army of the Assyrians, <hi type="italic">and all the idols shall be laid desolate. Samaria and her idols</hi> were ruined together by Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">Isa. x. 11</reference>), and <hi type="italic">their gods cast into the fire,</hi> for <hi type="italic">they were no gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.19">Isa. xxxvii. 19</reference>); and this was the Lord's doing: <hi type="italic">I will lay the idols desolate.</hi> Note, If the law of God prevail not to make men in authority destroy idols, God will take the work into his own hands, and will do it himself. 2. The gifts that passed between them and their gods shall be destroyed; for <hi type="italic">all the hires thereof shall be burnt with fire,</hi> which may be meant either of the presents they made to their idols for the replenishing of their altars, and the adorning of their statues and temples (these shall become a prey to the victorious army, which shall rifle not only private houses, but the houses of their gods), or of the corn, and wine, and oil, which they called the <hi type="italic">rewards,</hi> or <hi type="italic">hires,</hi> which <hi type="italic">their idols,</hi> their <hi type="italic">lovers,</hi> gave them (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.12">Hos. ii. 12</reference>); these shall be taken from them by him whom (by ascribing them to their dear idols) they had defrauded of the honour due to him. Note, That cannot prosper by which men either are hired to sin or hire others to sin; for <hi type="italic">the wages of sin</hi> will be <hi type="italic">death. She gathered it of the hire of the harlot,</hi> and <hi type="italic">it shall return to the hire of a harlot.</hi> They enriched themselves by their leagues with the idolatrous nations, who gave them advantages, to court them into the service of their idols, and their idols' temples were enriched with gifts by those who went a whoring after them. And all this wealth shall become a prey to the idolatrous nations, and so be the <hi type="italic">hire of a harlot</hi> again, wages to an army of idolaters, who shall take it as a reward given them by their gods. <hi type="italic">It shall be a present to king Jareb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">Hos. x. 6</reference>. What they gave to their idols, and what they thought they got by them, shall be as the hire of a harlot; the curse of God shall be upon it, and it shall never prosper, nor do them any good. It is common that what is squeezed out by one lust is squandered away upon another.
entries.2e3b9e158ccc10f290d26f94254671fe3822c190: <div eID="gen20395" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 743.)</title> <div sID="gen20396" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore I will wail and howl, I will go stripped and naked: I will make a wailing like the dragons, and mourning as the owls. <hi type="super">9</hi> For her wound <hi type="italic">is</hi> incurable; for it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> Declare ye <hi type="italic">it</hi> not at Gath, weep ye not at all: in the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust. <hi type="super">11</hi> Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked: the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth in the mourning of Beth-ezel; he shall receive of you his standing. <hi type="super">12</hi> For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto the gate of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">13</hi> O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast: she <hi type="italic">is</hi> the beginning of the sin to the daughter of Zion: for the transgressions of Israel were found in thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath: the houses of Achzib <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a lie to the kings of Israel. <hi type="super">15</hi> Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah: he shall come unto Adullam the glory of Israel. <hi type="super">16</hi> Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee. <div eID="gen20396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20397" type="x-p"/> We have here a long train of mourners attending the funeral of a ruined kingdom. <div eID="gen20397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20398" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet is himself chief mourner (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.8-Mic.1.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will wail and howl; I will go stripped and naked,</hi> as a man distracted with grief. The prophets usually expressed their own grief for the public grievances, partly to mollify the predictions of them, and to make it appear that is was not out of ill-will that they denounced the judgments of God (so far were they from desiring the woeful day that they dreaded it more than any thing), partly to show how very dreadful and mournful the calamities would be, and to stir up in the people a holy fear of them, that by repentance they might turn away the wrath of God. Note, We ought to lament the punishments of sinners as well as the sufferings of saints in this world; the weeping prophet did so (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer. ix. 1</reference>); so did this prophet. He <hi type="italic">makes a wailing like the dragons,</hi> or rather the <hi type="italic">jackals,</hi> ravenous beasts that in those countries used to meet in the night, and <hi type="italic">howl,</hi> and make <hi type="italic">hideous noises;</hi> he mourns <hi type="italic">as the owls,</hi> the <hi type="italic">screech-owls,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ostriches,</hi> as some read it. Two things the prophet here thus dolefully laments:—1. That Israel's case is desperate: <hi type="italic">Her wound is incurable;</hi> it is ruin without remedy; man cannot help her; God will not, because she will not by repentance and reformation help herself. There is indeed balm in Gilead and a physician there; but they will not apply to the physician, nor apply the balm to themselves, and therefore <hi type="italic">the wound is incurable.</hi> 2. That Judah likewise is in danger. The cup is going round, and is now put into Judah's hand: <hi type="italic">The enemy has come to the gate of Jerusalem.</hi> Soon after the destruction of Samaria and the ten tribes, the Assyrian army, under Sennacherib, laid siege to Jerusalem, came to the gate, but could not force their way any further; however, it was with great concern and trouble that the prophet foresaw the fright, so dearly did he love the peace of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen20398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20399" type="x-p"/> II. Several places are here brought in mourning, and are called upon to mourn; but with this proviso, that they should not let the Philistines hear them (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Declare it not in Gath;</hi> this is borrowed from David's lamentation for Saul and Jonathan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.20">2 Sam. i. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">Tell it not in Gath,</hi> for the uncircumcised will triumph in Israel's tears. Note, One would not, if it could be helped, gratify those that make themselves and their companions merry with the sins or with the sorrows of God's Israel. David was silent, and stifled his griefs, when <hi type="italic">the wicked were before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>. But, though it may be prudent not to give way to a noisy sorrow, yet it is duty to admit a silent one when the church of God is in distress. "<hi type="italic">Roll thyself in the dust</hi>" (as great mourners used to do) "and so let the house of Judah and every house in Jerusalem become a <hi type="italic">house of Aphrah,</hi> a <hi type="italic">house of dust,</hi> covered with dust, crumbled into dust." When God makes the house dust it becomes us to humble ourselves under his mighty hand, and to put our mouths in the dust, thus accommodating ourselves to the providences that concern us. Dust we are; God brings us to the dust, that we may know it, and own it. Divers other places are here named that should be sharers in this universal mourning, the names of some of which we do not find elsewhere, whence it is conjectured that they are names put upon them by the prophet, the signification of which might either indicate or aggravate the miseries coming upon them, thereby to awaken this secure and stupid people to a holy fear of divine wrath. We find Sennacherib's invasion thus described, in the prediction of it, by the impressions of terror it should make upon the several cities that fell in his way, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.28-Isa.10.29">Isa. x. 28, 29</reference>, &c. Let us observe the particulars here, 1. <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Saphir,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">neat</hi> and <hi type="italic">beautiful (thou that dwellest fairly,</hi> so the margin reads it), shall <hi type="italic">pass away</hi> into captivity, or be forced to flee, stripped of all their ornaments <hi type="italic">and having their shame naked.</hi> Note, Those who appear ever so fine and delicate know not what contempt they may be exposed to; and the more grievous will the shame be to those who have been inhabitants of Saphir. 2. <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Zaanan,</hi> which signifies the <hi type="italic">country of flocks,</hi> a populous country, where the people are as numerous and thick as flocks of sheep, shall yet be so taken up with their own calamities, felt or feared, that they shall <hi type="italic">not come forth in the mourning of Bethezel,</hi> which signifies a <hi type="italic">place near,</hi> shall not condole with, nor bring any succour to, their next neighbours in distress; for <hi type="italic">he shall receive of you his standing;</hi> the enemy shall encamp among you, O inhabitants of Zaanan! shall take up a station there, shall find footing among you. Those may well think themselves excused from helping their neighbours who find they have enough to do to help themselves and to hold their own. 3. As for <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Maroth</hi> (which, some think, is put for Ramoth, others that it signifies the <hi type="italic">rough places</hi>), they <hi type="italic">waited carefully for good,</hi> and were grieved for the want of it, but were disappointed; for <hi type="italic">evil came from the Lord unto the gate of Jerusalem,</hi> when the Assyrian army besieged it, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.12">v. 12</reference>. The inhabitants of Maroth might well overlook their own particular grievances when they saw the holy city itself in danger, and might well overlook the Assyrian, that was the instrument, when they saw the evil coming <hi type="italic">from the Lord.</hi> 4. Lachish was a city of Judah, which Sennacherib laid siege to, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1-Isa.36.2">Isa. xxxvi. 1,2</reference>. The inhabitants of that city are called to <hi type="italic">bind the chariot to the swift beast,</hi> to prepare for a speedy flight, as having no other way left to secure themselves and their families; or it is spoken ironically: "You have had your chariots and your swift beasts, but where are they now?" God's quarrel with Lachish is that she is <hi type="italic">the beginning of sin,</hi> probably the sin of idolatry, <hi type="italic">to the daughter of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.13">v. 13</reference>); they had learned it from the ten tribes, their near neighbours, and so infected the two tribes with it. Note, Those that help to bring sin into a country do but thereby prepare for the throwing of themselves out of it. Those must expect to be first in the punishment who have been ringleaders in sin. <hi type="italic">The transgressions of Israel were found in thee;</hi> when they came to be traced up to their original they were found to take rise very much from that city. God knows at whose door to lay the blame of the transgressions of Israel, and whom to find guilty. Lachish, having been so much accessory to the sin of Israel, shall certainly be reckoned with: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt give presents to Moresheth-gath,</hi> a city of the Philistines, which perhaps had a dependence upon Gath, that famous Philistine city; thou shalt send to court those of that city to assist thee, but it shall be in vain, for (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.14">v. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">the houses of Achzib</hi> (a city which joined to Mareshah, or Moresheth, and is mentioned with it, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Josh. xv. 44</reference>) <hi type="italic">shall be a lie to the kings of Israel;</hi> though they depend upon their strength, yet they shall fail them. Here there is an allusion to the name. <hi type="italic">Achzib</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">a lie,</hi> and so it shall prove to those that trust in it. 5. Mareshah, that could not, or would not, help Israel, shall herself be made a prey (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will bring a heir</hi> (that is, an enemy) that shall take possession of thy lands, with as much assurance as if he were heir at law to them, and <hi type="italic">he shall come to Adullam,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to the glory of Israel,</hi> that is, to Jerusalem the head city;" or "<hi type="italic">The glory of Israel</hi> shall come to be as Adullam, a poor despicable place;" or, "The king of Assyria, whom Israel had gloried in, shall come to Adullam, in laying the country waste." 6. The whole land of Judah seems to be spoken to (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.16">v. 16</reference>) and called to weeping and mourning: "<hi type="italic">Make thee bald,</hi> by tearing thy hair and shaving thy head; <hi type="italic">poll thee for thy delicate children,</hi> that had been tenderly and nicely brought up; <hi type="italic">enlarge thy baldness as the eagle</hi> when she casts her feathers and is all over bald; <hi type="italic">for they have gone into captivity from thee,</hi> and are not likely to return; and their captivity will be the more grievous to them because they have been brought up delicately and have not been inured to hardship." Or this is directed particularly to the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Mareshah,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">v. 15</reference>. That was the prophet's own city, and yet he denounces the judgments of God against it; for it shall be an aggravation of its sin that it had such a prophet, and knew not the day of its visitation. Its being thus privileged, since it improved not the privilege, shall not procure favour for it either with God or with his prophet.  <chapter eID="Mic.1"/> <div eID="gen20399" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a55c1434735cd8f54f54980a7706fed47d8ba07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12716"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> Micah was a native of Moresheth, not the same as Mareshah in <reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">Mi 1:15</reference>, but the town called Moresheth-gath (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.14">Mi 1:14</reference>), which lay near Eleutheropolis, west of Jerusalem, on the border of the Philistine country; so called to distinguish it from Moresheth of Judah. His full name is Micaiah (not the Micaiah mentioned <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">1Ki 22:8</reference>, the son of Imlah), signifying, Who is like Jehovah? The time of his prophesying is stated in the introduction to be in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, that is, between 757 and 699 B.C. Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jr 26:18</reference>) quotes <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>, as delivered in the reign of Hezekiah. He was thus a contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea. The idolatries practised in the reign of Ahaz accord with Micah's denunciations of such gross evils, and confirm the truth of the time assigned <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>. His prophecies are partly against Israel (Samaria), partly against Judah. As Samaria, Israel's metropolis, was taken first, and Jerusalem, the capital of Judah subsequently, in the introductory heading, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>, Samaria is put first, then Jerusalem. He prophesies the capture of both; the Jews' captivity and restoration; and the coming and reign of Messiah. His style is full, round, and perspicuous; his diction pure, and his parallelisms regular. His description of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">19</reference>) is not surpassed by any elsewhere in Scripture. The similarity between Isaiah and Micah in some passages (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.3">Mi 4:1-3</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>) is to be accounted for by their being contemporaries, acquainted with each other's inspired writings, and having the same subjects for their theme. Hengstenberg maintains that the passage in Micah is the original. Isaiah was somewhat the older, being a prophet in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham's predecessor, whereas Micah began his prophecies under Jotham.<div eID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23521" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> The book consists of two parts: (1) the first through fifth chapters; (2) the sixth and seventh chapters, a dialogue or contestation between Jehovah and His people, in which He reproaches them with their unnatural and ungrateful conduct, and threatens judgment for their corruptions, but consoles them with the promise of restoration from captivity.<div eID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> Micah stands sixth of the minor prophets in the Hebrew canon, but third in the Septuagint.<div eID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.1.1-Mic.1.16">Mi 1:1-16</reference>. God's Wrath against Samaria and Judah; the Former Is to Be Overthrown; Such Judgments in Prospect Call for Mourning.</title> <div sID="gen23525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12716"/>[]
entries.20db62566058c1d8609c3cf38f7f4356496253aa: <hi type="bold">2. all that therein is--</hi>Hebrew, "whatever fills it." Micaiah, son of Imlah, our prophet's namesake, begins his prophecy similarly, "Hearken, O people, every one of you." Micah designedly uses the same preface, implying that his ministrations are a continuation of his predecessor's of the same name. Both probably had before their mind Moses' similar attestation of heaven and earth in a like case (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.28">De 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">32:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God be witness against you--</hi>namely, that none of you can say, when the time of your punishment shall come, that you were not forewarned. The punishment denounced is stated in <reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">Mi 1:3</reference>, &c.<div eID="gen23526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from his holy temple--</hi>that is, heaven (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.30">1Ki 8:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">Ro 1:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23527" type="x-p"/>
entries.9145466a65f573187730b2f9e098db3bba89faac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12717"/><div sID="gen23528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12717"/><hi type="bold">3. tread upon the high places of the earth--</hi>He shall destroy the fortified heights (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">33:29</reference>) [Grotius]. <div eID="gen23528" type="x-p"/>
entries.809406fa6f7a964627c489a1b0df0acfffbc503c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12718"/><div sID="gen23529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12718"/>4. Imagery from earthquakes and volcanic agency, to describe the terrors which attend Jehovah's coming in judgment (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.5.5">Jud 5:5</reference>). Neither men of high degree, as the mountains, nor men of low degree, as the valleys, can secure themselves or their land from the judgments of God.<div eID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as wax--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">Psa 97:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.3">Is 64:1-3</reference>). The third clause, "as wax," &c., answers to the first in the parallelism, "the mountains shall be molten"; the fourth, "as the waters," &c., to the second, "the valleys shall be cleft." As wax melts by fire, so the mountains before God, at His approach; and as waters poured down a steep cannot stand but are diffused abroad, so the valleys shall be cleft before Jehovah. <div eID="gen23530" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3ddd3a8b5245a9bcd868e378755e446bb3870b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12719"/><div sID="gen23531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12719"/><hi type="bold">5. For the transgression of Jacob is all this--</hi>All these terrors attending Jehovah's coming are caused by the sins of Jacob or Israel, that is, the whole people.<div eID="gen23531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">What is the transgression of Jacob?--</hi>Taking up the question often in the mouths of the people when reproved, "What is our transgression?" (compare Mal <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.7">1:6, 7</reference>), He answers, Is it not Samaria? Is not that city (the seat of the calf-worship) the cause of Jacob's apostasy (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.16">1Ki 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.26">15:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.13">16:13</reference>, 19, 25, 30)?<div eID="gen23532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and what are the high places of Judah?--</hi>What city is the cause of the idolatries on the high places of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.4">2Ki 18:4</reference>)? <div eID="gen23533" type="x-p"/>
entries.734791fa850a82152998c634bbfd4bf6106791f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12720"/><div sID="gen23534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12720"/>6. Samaria's punishment is mentioned first, as it was to fall before Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as an heap of the field--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>). Such a heap of stones and rubbish as is gathered out of fields, to clear them (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Ho 12:11</reference>). Palestine is of a soil abounding in stones, which are gathered out before the vines are planted (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as plantings of a vineyard--</hi>as a place where vines are planted. Vineyards were cultivated on the sides of hills exposed to the sun. The hill on which Samaria was built by Omri, had been, doubtless, planted with vines originally; now it is to be reduced again to its original state (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.24">1Ki 16:24</reference>).<div eID="gen23536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pour down--</hi>dash down the stones of the city into the valley beneath. A graphic picture of the present appearance of the ruins, which is as though "the buildings of the ancient city had been thrown down from the brow of the hill" [Scottish Mission of Inquiry, pp. 293,294].<div eID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">discover the foundations--</hi>destroy it so utterly as to lay bare its foundations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.14">Eze 13:14</reference>). Samaria was destroyed by Shalmaneser. <div eID="gen23538" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2afb4d422d0e149146fec50b4f60eb2d456cff6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12721"/><div sID="gen23539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12721"/><hi type="bold">7. all the hires--</hi>the wealth which Israel boasted of receiving from her idols as the "rewards" or "hire" for worshipping them (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.5">Ho 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">idols ... will I ... desolate--</hi>that is, give them up to the foe to strip off the silver and gold with which they are overlaid.<div eID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot--</hi>Israel gathered (made for herself) her idols from the gold and silver received from false gods, as she thought, the "hire" of her worshipping them; and they shall again become what they had been before, the hire of spiritual harlotry, that is, the prosperity of the foe, who also being worshippers of idols will ascribe the acquisition to their idols [Maurer]. Grotius explains it, The offerings sent to Israel's temple by the Assyrians, whose idolatry Israel adopted, shall go back to the Assyrians, her teachers in idolatry, as the hire or fee for having taught it. The image of a harlot's hire for the supposed temporal reward of spiritual fornication, is more common in Scripture (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Ho 9:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23541" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ce81109ca188729e799f03e0d7e6748f0e170ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12722"/><div sID="gen23542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12722"/><hi type="bold">8. Therefore I will wail--</hi>The prophet first shows how the coming judgment affects himself, in order that he might affect the minds of his countrymen similarly.<div eID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stripped--</hi>that is, of shoes, or sandals, as the Septuagint translates. Otherwise "naked" would be a tautology.<div eID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">naked--</hi>"Naked" means divested of the upper garment (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Is 20:2</reference>). "Naked and barefoot," the sign of mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). The prophet's upper garment was usually rough and coarse-haired (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.8">2Ki 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.4">Zec 13:4</reference>).<div eID="gen23544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like the dragons--</hi>so Jerome. Rather, "the wild dogs," jackals or wolves, which wail like an infant when in distress or alone [Maurer]. (See on <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>).<div eID="gen23545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">owls--</hi>rather, "ostriches," which give a shrill and long-drawn, sigh-like cry, especially at night. <div eID="gen23546" type="x-p"/>
entries.10c5bc12a59df35a2bd2bdb4b948465650a1fa07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12723"/><div sID="gen23547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12723"/><hi type="bold">9. wound ... incurable--</hi>Her case, politically and morally, is desperate (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>).<div eID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is come--</hi>the wound, or impending calamity (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.28">Is 10:28</reference>).<div eID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is come ... even to Jerusalem--</hi>The evil is no longer limited to Israel. The prophet foresees Sennacherib coming even "to the gate" of the principal city. The use of "it" and "he" is appropriately distinct. "It," the calamity, "came unto" Judah, many of the inhabitants of which suffered, but did not reach the citizens of Jerusalem, "the gate" of which the foe ("he") "came unto," but did not enter (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Is 36:1</reference>;<reference osisRef="Isa.37.33-Isa.37.37">37:33-37</reference>). <div eID="gen23549" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8451be2e84726813fcd3bfc9646f27573e050fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12724"/><div sID="gen23550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12724"/><hi type="bold">10. Declare ye it not at Gath--</hi>on the borders of Judea, one of the five cities of the Philistines, who would exult at the calamity of the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.20">2Sa 1:20</reference>). Gratify not those who exult over the falls of the Israel of God.<div eID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weep ye not at all--</hi>Do not betray your inward sorrow by outward weeping, within the cognizance of the enemy, lest they should exult at it. Reland translates, "Weep not in Acco," that is, Ptolemais, now St. Jean d'Acre, near the foot of Mount Carmel; allotted to Asher, but never occupied by that tribe (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.31">Jud 1:31</reference>); Acco's inhabitants would, therefore, like Gath's, rejoice at Israel's disaster. Thus the parallelism is best carried out in all the three clauses of the verse, and there is a similar play on sounds in each, in the Hebrew Gath, resembling in sound the Hebrew for "declare"; Acco, resembling the Hebrew for "weep"; and Aphrah, meaning "dust." While the Hebrews were not to expose their misery to foreigners, they ought to bewail it in their own cities, for example, Aphrah or Ophrah (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.23">Jos 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.17">1Sa 13:17</reference>), in the tribe of Benjamin. To "roll in the dust" marked deep sorrow (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jr 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.30">Eze 27:30</reference>). <div eID="gen23551" type="x-p"/>
entries.d524c7b99a26dca4290560773a1d8c24a8a255c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12725"/><div sID="gen23552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12725"/><hi type="bold">11. Pass ye away--</hi>that is, Thou shall go into captivity.<div eID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inhabitant of Saphir--</hi>a village amidst the hills of Judah, between Eleutheropolis and Ascalon, called so, from the Hebrew word for "beauty." Though thy name be "beauty," which heretofore was thy characteristic, thou shalt have thy "shame" made "naked." This city shall be dismantled of its walls, which are the garments, as it were, of cities; its citizens also shall be hurried into captivity, with persons exposed (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Is 47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.37">Eze 16:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.10">Ho 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth--</hi>Its inhabitants did not come forth to console the people of Beth-ezel in their mourning, because the calamity was universal; none was exempt from it (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.25">Jr 6:25</reference>). "Zaanan" is the same as Zenan, in Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.37">Jos 15:37</reference>), meaning the "place of flocks." The form of the name used is made like the Hebrew for "came forth." Though in name seeming to imply that thou dost come forth, thou "camest not forth."<div eID="gen23554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-ezel--</hi>perhaps Azal (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zec 14:5</reference>), near Jerusalem. It means a "house on the side," or "near." Though so near, as its name implies, to Zaanan, Beth-ezel received no succor or sympathy from Zaanan.<div eID="gen23555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall receive of you his standing--</hi>"he," that is, the foe; "his standing," that is, his sustenance [Piscator]. Or, "he shall be caused a delay by you, Zaanan." He shall be brought to a stand for a time in besieging you; hence it is said just before, "Zaanan came not forth," that is, shut herself up within her walls to withstand a siege. But it was only for a time. She, too, fell like Beth-ezel before her [Vatablus]. Maurer construes thus: "The inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth; the mourning of Beth-ezel takes away from you her shelter." Though Beth-ezel be at your side (that is, near), according to her name, yet as she also mourns under the oppression of the foe, she cannot give you shelter, or be at your side as a helper (as her name might lead you to expect), if you come forth and be intercepted by him from returning to Zaanan. <div eID="gen23556" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc5d45ad592d9b664b662cdae24a5f25ad88b696: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12726"/><div sID="gen23557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12726"/><hi type="bold">12. Maroth--</hi>possibly the same as Maarath (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.59">Jos 15:59</reference>). Perhaps a different town, lying between the previously mentioned towns and the capital, and one of those plundered by Rab-shakeh on his way to it.<div eID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waited carefully for good--</hi>that is, for better fortune, but in vain [Calvin]. Gesenius translates, "is grieved for her goods," "taken away" from her. This accords with the meaning of Maroth, "bitterness," to which allusion is made in "is grieved." But the antithesis favors English Version, "waited carefully (that is, anxiously) for good, but evil came down."<div eID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the Lord--</hi>not from chance.<div eID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the gate of Jerusalem--</hi>after the other cities of Judah have been taken. <div eID="gen23560" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9ae9902859cb4f4df4b85804c0bb9c885082cb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12727"/><div sID="gen23561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12727"/>13. "Bind the chariot to the swift steed," in order by a hasty flight to escape the invading foe. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.36.2">Is 36:2</reference>, on "Lachish," at which Sennacherib fixed his headquarters (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2Ki 18:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jr 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she is the beginning of the sin to ... Zion--</hi>Lachish was the first of the cities of Judah, according to this passage, to introduce the worship of false gods, imitating what Jeroboam had introduced in Israel. As lying near the border of the north kingdom, Lachish was first to be infected by its idolatry, which thence spread to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen23562" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1b2222df684e9a005a08c4fee5805491319b341: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12728"/><div sID="gen23563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12728"/><hi type="bold">14. shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath--</hi>that its inhabitants may send thee help. Maurer explains it, "thou shalt give a writing of renunciation to Moresheth-gath," that is, thou shalt renounce all claim to it, being compelled to yield it up to the foe. "Thou," that is, Judah. "Israel" in this verse is used for the kingdom of Judah, which was the chief representative of the whole nation of Israel. Moresheth-gath is so called because it had fallen for a time under the power of the neighboring Philistines of Gath. It was the native town of Micah (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Achzib--</hi>meaning "lying." Achzib, as its name implies, shall prove a "lie to ... Israel," that is, shall disappoint Israel's hopes of succor from her (compare <reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.20">Job 6:15-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">Jr 15:18</reference>). Achzib was in Judah between Keilah and Mareshah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>). Perhaps the same as Chezib (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.5">Ge 38:5</reference>). <div eID="gen23564" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5800a931d891ad1b3d79d3dbcffa270a79d0d56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12729"/><div sID="gen23565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12729"/><hi type="bold">15. Yet will I bring an heir unto thee--</hi>rather, "the heir." As thou art now occupied by possessors who expelled the former inhabitants, so will I bring "yet" again the new possessor, namely, the Assyrian foe. Other heirs will supplant us in every inheritance but that of heaven. There is a play upon the meaning of Mareshah, "an inheritance": there shall come the new heir of the inheritance.<div eID="gen23565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Adullam the glory of Israel--</hi>so called as being superior in situation; when it and the neighboring cities fell, Israel's glory was gone. Maurer, as the Margin, translates, "the glory of Israel" (her chief citizens: answering to "thy delicate children," <reference osisRef="Mic.1.16">Mi 1:16</reference>) "shall come in flight to Adullam." English Version better preserves the parallelism, "the heir" in the first clause answering to "he" in the second. <div eID="gen23566" type="x-p"/>
entries.055d253d336777cceab92c50087a21b5bf35ad06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12730"/><div sID="gen23567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12730"/><hi type="bold">16. Make thee bald, &c.--</hi>a token of deep mourning (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.3">Ezr 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.20">Job 1:20</reference>). Mourn, O land, for thy darling children.<div eID="gen23567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poll--</hi>shave off thy hair.<div eID="gen23568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enlarge thy baldness--</hi>Mourn grievously. The land is compared to a mother weeping for her children.<div eID="gen23569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the eagle--</hi>the bald eagle, or the dark-winged vulture. In the moulting season all eagles are comparatively bald (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>). <chapter eID="Mic.1"/>

entries.63d5211126dbc17e3dbd8ff03a1ba4e7270b9ef5: <div eID="gen34683" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of the Prophet Micah</title> <div sID="gen34684" type="x-p"/> Micah, the Morasthite, or of Moresa, a village near the city Eleutheropolis, in the southern part of Judah, is the sixth in order of the twelve minor prophets. He prophesied under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, for about fifty years. Some have confounded him with Micaiah, son of Imlah, who lived in the kingdom of the ten tribes, under the reign of Ahab. <div eID="gen34684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34685" type="x-p"/> The spurious Dorotheus says that Micah was buried in the burying-place of the Anakim, whose habitation had been at Hebron, and round about it. This prophet appeared almost at the same time with Isaiah, and has even borrowed some expressions from him. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa 2:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mic 4:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.41.15">Isa 41:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mic 4:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34686" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of Micah contains but seven chapters. He foretells the calamities of Samaria, which was taken by Shalmaneser, and reduced to a heap of stones. Afterwards he prophesies against Judah, and declares the troubles that Sennacherib should bring upon it under the reign of Hezekiah. Then he declaims against the iniquities of Samaria. He foretells the captivity of the ten tribes, and their return into their own country. The third chapter contains a pathetic invective against the princes of the house of Jacob, and the judges of the house of Israel; which seems leveled against the chief of the kingdom of Judah, the judges, the magistrates, the priests, the false prophets, etc. He upbraids them with their avarice, their injustice, and falsehood; and tells them they will be the occasion that Jerusalem shall be reduced to a heap of rubbish, and the mountain of the temple shall be as a forest. We are informed, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.19">Jer 26:19</reference>, that this prophecy was pronounced in the reign of Hezekiah; and that it saved Jeremiah from death. <div eID="gen34686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34687" type="x-p"/> After these terrible denunciations, Micah speaks of the reign of the Messiah, and of the establishment of the Christian Church. And as the peaceable times which succeeded the return from the Babylonish captivity, and which were a figure of the reign of the Messiah, were disturbed by a tempest of a short continuance, Micah foretold it in such a manner as agrees very well with what Ezekiel says of the war of Gog against the Jews. Micah speaks in particular of the birth of the Messiah; that he was to be born at Bethlehem; and that his dominion was to extend to the utmost parts of the earth. He says that God should raise seven shepherds, who should reign by the sword over Assyria, and in the land of Nimrod; which Calmet explains of Darius, son of Hystaspes; and of the seven confederates that killed the magian, and who possessed the empire of the Persians, after the extinction of the family of Cyrus. The fifth chapter, from verse 7 to the end, describes the flourishing estate of the Jews in their own country, from the reign of Darius, and after the Maccabees; yet in such a manner, that he mingles several things in it that can apply only to the Church of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen34687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34688" type="x-p"/> The two last chapters of Micah contain, first, a long invective against the iniquities of Samaria: then he foretells the fall of Babylon; the re-establishment of the cities of Israel; the greatness of the country possessed by the Israelites; their happiness; the graces wherewith God will favor them; and all this in such lofty terms, that they chiefly agree with the Christian Church. St. Jerome says that Micah was buried at Morasthi, ten furlongs from Eleutheropolis; and Sozomenes says that his tomb was revealed to Zebennus, bishop of Eleutheropolis, under the reign of Theodosius the Great. He calls the place of his burial Beretsate, which is probably the same as Morasthi, ten furlongs from Eleutheropolis. <div eID="gen34688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34689" type="x-p"/> Bishop Newcome observes that Micah was of the kingdom of Judah, as he only makes mention of kings who reigned over that country. It is supposed that he prophesied farther on in the reign of Hezekiah than Hosea did; although <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mic 5:5</reference> was written before the captivity of the ten tribes, which happened in the sixth year of Hezekiah. It is plain from <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mic 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">Mic 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.9">Mic 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.12">Mic 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.13">Mic 1:13</reference>, that he was sent both to Israel and Judah. Like Amos and Hosea, he reproves and threatens, with great spirit and energy, a corrupt people. See <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1-Mic.2.3">Mic 2:1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.8">Mic 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.9">Mic 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mic 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.2-Mic.3.4">Mic 3:2-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.6">Mic 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.10-Mic.3.12">Mic 3:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2-Mic.7.4">Mic 7:2-4</reference>. And, like Hosea, he inveighs against the princes and prophets with the highest indignation. See <reference osisRef="Mic.3.5-Mic.3.7">Mic 3:5-7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.9-Mic.3.12">Mic 3:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.3">Mic 7:3</reference>. The reader will observe that these similar topics are treated of by each prophet with remarkable variety, and copiousness of expression. <div eID="gen34689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34690" type="x-p"/> Some of his prophecies are distinct and illustrious ones, as <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mic 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mic 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.4">Mic 4:1-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.10">Mic 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2-Mic.5.4">Mic 5:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mic 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8-Mic.7.10">Mic 7:8-10</reference>. <div eID="gen34690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34691" type="x-p"/> We may justly admire the elegance of his diction: - <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mic 2:12</reference> - "I will surely gather, O Jacob, all of thee:I will surely assemble the residue of Israel.I will put them together as sheep of Bozra,As a flock in the midst of their fold:They shall make a tumult from the multitude of men. <reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mic 2:13</reference> - He that forceth a passage is come up before them:They have forced a passage, and have passed through the gate; and are gone forth by it:And their King passeth before them, even Jehovah at the head of them." <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mic 4:1</reference> - "But it shall come to pass, in the latter days,That the mountain of the temple of Jehovah shall beEstablished on the top of the mountains,And it shall be exalted above the hills;And the people shall flow into it: <reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">Mic 4:2</reference> - And many nations shall go, and shall say,Come, and let us go up unto the mountain of Jehovah,And unto the temple of the God of Jacob:That he may teach us of his ways, and that we may walk in his paths. For from Sion shall go forth a law,And the word of Jehovah from Jerusalem. <reference osisRef="Mic.4.3">Mic 4:3</reference> - And he shall judge between many people,And he shall convince strong nations afar off:And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares,And their spears into pruninghooks:Nation shall not lift up sword against nation,Neither shall they any longer learn war." <div eID="gen34691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34692" type="x-p"/> His animation - <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">Mic 1:5</reference>, lines 3, 4 - "What is the transgression of Jacob? - is it not that of Samaria?And what are the high places of Judah? - are they not those of Jerusalem?" <reference osisRef="Mic.4.9">Mic 4:9</reference> - "And now why dost thou cry out loudly?Is there no king in thee?Hath thy counsellor perished?For pangs have seized thee, as a woman in travail." <div eID="gen34692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34693" type="x-p"/> There are few beauties of composition of which examples may not be found in this prophet. For sublimity and impressiveness in several places, he is unrivalled. The Lord's controversy, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.1-Mic.6.8">Mic 6:1-8</reference>, is equal to any thing even in the prophet Isaiah. It has a powerful effect on every attentive reader. <div eID="gen34693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34694" type="x-p"/> His strength of expression: - <reference osisRef="Mic.1.6">Mic 1:6</reference> - "Therefore will I make Samaria a heap of the field, a place for the plantings of a vineyard:And I will pour down her stones into the valley, and I will discover her foundations." <reference osisRef="Mic.3.2">Mic 3:2</reference> - "Ye who hate good and love evil:Who pluck their skin from off them,And their flesh from off their bones." <reference osisRef="Mic.3.3">Mic 3:3</reference> - Who have also eaten the flesh of my people,And have flayed their skin from off them,And have broken their bones;And have divided them asunder, as flesh in the pot:And as meat within the caldron." <reference osisRef="Mic.7.1">Mic 7:1</reference> - "Wo is me; for I am becomeAs the gatherers of late figs, as the gleaners of the vintage.There is no cluster to eat:My soul desireth the first-ripe fig. <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mic 7:2</reference> - The good man is perished from the land,And there is none upright among men.All of them lie in wait for blood;They hunt every man his brother for his destruction." <div eID="gen34694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34695" type="x-p"/> His pathos: - <reference osisRef="Mic.1.16">Mic 1:16</reference> - "Make thee bald, and cut off thine hair for thy delicate children;Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle;For they are gone into captivity from thee." <reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mic 2:4</reference> - "In that day shall a proverb be taken up against you;And a grievous lamentation shall be made:Saying, 'We are utterly laid waste:He hath changed the portion of my people:How hath he departed from me,To bring again him that divided our fields!'" <div eID="gen34695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34696" type="x-p"/> His sublimity: - <reference osisRef="Mic.1.2">Mic 1:2</reference> - "Hear, O ye people, all of you:Hearken, O land, and all that are therein.And let the Lord Jehovah be witness against you;Even the Lord from his holy temple. <reference osisRef="Mic.1.3">Mic 1:3</reference> - For, behold, Jehovah will go forth from his place:And he will come down, and will tread upon the high places of the earth. <reference osisRef="Mic.1.4">Mic 1:4</reference> - And the mountains shall be molten under him;And the valleys shall cleave asunder;As wax before the fire, As waters poured down a steep place." <reference osisRef="Mic.6.1">Mic 6:1</reference> - "Hear ye now what Jehovah saith:Arise, contend thou before the mountains;And let the hills hear thy voice." <reference osisRef="Mic.7.16">Mic 7:16</reference> - "The nations shall see, and shall be confounded because of their might:They shall lay their hand upon their mouth; their ears shall be deaf. <reference osisRef="Mic.7.17">Mic 7:17</reference> - They shall lick the dust as the serpent;As the creeping things upon the earth, they shall tremble from their close places:Because of Jehovah our God, they shall stand in awe; and they shall fear because of thee." <div eID="gen34696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34697" type="x-p"/> The prophet begins with calling the attention of all people to the awful descent of Jehovah, coming to execute his judgments against the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1-Mic.1.5">Mic 1:1-5</reference>; first against Samaria, whose fate the prophet laments on the dress of mourners, and with the doleful cries of the fox or ostrich, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.6-Mic.1.8">Mic 1:6-8</reference>; and then against Jerusalem, which is threatened with the invasion of Sennacherib. Other cities of Judah are likewise threatened; and their danger represented to be so great as to oblige them to have recourse for protection even to their enemies the Philistines, from whom they desired at first to conceal their situation. But all resources are declared to be vain; Israel and Judah must go into captivity, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.9-Mic.1.16">Mic 1:9-16</reference>. <div eID="gen34697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34698" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34699" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord that came to Micah the Morasthite - For all authentic particulars relative to this prophet, see the introduction. <div eID="gen34699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34700" type="x-p"/> In the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah - These three kings reigned about threescore years; and Micah is supposed to have prophesied about forty or fifty years; but no more of his prophecies have reached posterity than what are contained in this book, nor is there any evidence that any more was written. His time appears to have been spent chiefly in preaching and exhorting; and he was directed to write those parts only that were calculated to profit succeeding generations.
entries.60663a1bb47a4139383778c09b140fbc76f170fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34701" type="x-p"/> Hear, all ye people - The very commencement of this prophecy supposes preceding exhortations and predictions. <div eID="gen34701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34702" type="x-p"/> Hearken, O earth - ארץ arets, here, should be translated land, the country of the Hebrews being only intended. <div eID="gen34702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34703" type="x-p"/> And let the Lord God be Witness - Let him who has sent me with this message be witness that I have delivered it faithfully; and be a witness against you, if you take not the warning. <div eID="gen34703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34704" type="x-p"/> The Lord from his holy temple - The place where he still remains as your King, and your Judge; and where you profess to pay your devotions. The temple was yet standing, for Jerusalem was not taken for many years after this; and these prophecies were delivered before the captivity of the ten tribes, as Micah appears to have been sent both to Israel and to Judah. See <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5-Mic.1.9">Mic 1:5-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.12">Mic 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.13">Mic 1:13</reference>.
entries.000b4269bcb5c7254401ad8b4c2b974a595a3213: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34705" type="x-p"/> For, behold, the Lord cometh forth - See this clause, <reference osisRef="Amo.4.13">Amo 4:13</reference> (note). He represents Jehovah as a mighty conqueror, issuing from his pavilion, stepping from mountain to mountain, which rush down and fill the valleys before him; a consuming fire accompanying him, that melts and confounds every hill and dale, and blends all in universal confusion. God is here represented as doing that himself which other conquerors do by the multitude of their hosts; levelling the mountains, filling some of the valleys, and digging for waters in others, and pouring them from hills and dales for the use of the conquering armies, by pipes and aqueducts. <div eID="gen34705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34706" type="x-p"/> And why is all this mighty movement? <reference osisRef="Mic.1.5">Mic 1:5</reference>. "For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel."
entries.f109ab8f62c2f6820b08ed412549d1b0a61fc0de: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34707" type="x-p"/> What is the transgression of Jacob? - Is it not something extremely grievous? Is it not that of Samaria? Samaria and Jerusalem, the chief cities, are infected with idolatry. Each has its high places, and its idol worship, in opposition to the worship of the true God. That there was idolatry practiced by the elders of Israel, even in the temple of Jehovah, see <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>, etc. As the royal cities in both kingdoms gave the example of gross idolatry, no wonder that it spread through the whole land, both of Israel and Judah.
entries.4a848bd9c192a15abe8eca6f8de22885ab4097c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34708" type="x-p"/> I will make Samaria - I will bring it to desolation: and, instead of being a royal city, it shall be a place for vineyards. Newcome observes, that Samaria was situated on a hill, the right soil for a vineyard. <div eID="gen34708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34709" type="x-p"/> I will discover the foundations thereof - I will cause its walls and fortifications to be razed to the ground.
entries.a8befb7a701c9b412d9601ad326de5c642044eac: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34710" type="x-p"/> All the hires thereof shall be burned - Multitudes of women gave the money they gained by their public prostitution at the temples for the support of the priesthood, the ornamenting of the walls, altars, and images. So that these things, and perhaps several of the images themselves, were literally the hire of the harlots: and God threatens here to deliver all into the hands of enemies who should seize on this wealth, and literally spend it in the same way in which it was acquired; so that "to the hire of a harlot these things should return."
entries.6fc1136d8cfaa7dfd504f0d7b10db67d336d0b6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34711" type="x-p"/> I will make a wailing like the dragons - Newcome translates: - <div eID="gen34711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34712" type="x-p"/> I will make a wailing like the foxes, (or jackals), <div eID="gen34712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34713" type="x-p"/> And mourning like the daughters of the ostrich. <div eID="gen34713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34714" type="x-p"/> This beast, the jackal or shiagal, we have often met with in the prophets. Travellers inform us that its howlings by night are most lamentable; and as to the ostrich, it is remarkable for its fearful shrieking and agonizing groanings after night. Dr. Shaw says he has often heard them groan as if they were in the greatest agonies.
entries.4dbf84052e57b69e1c6166d8482bbf9c2e501e26: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34715" type="x-p"/> Her wound is incurable - Nothing shall prevent their utter ruin, for they have filled up the measure of their iniquity. <div eID="gen34715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34716" type="x-p"/> He is come - even to Jerusalem - The desolation and captivity of Israel shall first take place; that of Judah shall come after.
entries.7c6e9c2b825fc9c7833461af752798e36444fca1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34717" type="x-p"/> Declare ye it not at Gath - Do not let this prediction be known among the Philistines, else they will glory over you. <div eID="gen34717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34718" type="x-p"/> House of Aphrah - Or, Beth-aphrah. This place is mentioned <reference osisRef="Jos.18.23">Jos 18:23</reference>, as in the tribe of Benjamin. There is a paronomasia, or play on words, here: בבית לעפרה עפר bebeith leaphrah aphar, "Roll thyself in the dust in the house of dust."
entries.52a9bae6161d0bf58b98c1d658dde14201b63ccf: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34719" type="x-p"/> Inhabitant of Saphir - Sapher, Sepphoris, or Sephora, was the strongest place in Galilee. - Calmet. It was a city in the tribe of Judah, between Eleutheropolis and Ascalon. - Houbigant. <div eID="gen34719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34720" type="x-p"/> Zaanan - Another city in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.13">Jos 15:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34721" type="x-p"/> Beth-ezel - A place near Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Zac.14.5">Zac 14:5</reference>. Some think that Jerusalem itself is intended by this word.
entries.538e91124f45812725e98381ff86da7e9ec816f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34722" type="x-p"/> The inhabitant of Maroth - There was a city of a similar name in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.59">Jos 15:59</reference>.
entries.657580783024dc16326d8b27ca369f5660b42455: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34723" type="x-p"/> Inhabitant of Lachish - This city was in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.39">Jos 15:39</reference>, and was taken by Sennacherib when he was coming against Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Kgs 18:13</reference>, etc., and it is supposed that he wished to reduce this city first, that, possessing it, he might prevent Hezekiah's receiving any help from Egypt. <div eID="gen34723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34724" type="x-p"/> She is the beginning of the sin - This seems to intimate that Lachish was the first city in Judah which received the idolatrous worship of Israel.
